extraction.name: FLEURS
extraction.description: FLEURS, the Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech benchmark, is an n-way parallel speech dataset in 102 languages built on top of the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, with approximately 12 hours of speech supervision per language. It can be used for a variety of speech tasks, including Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Translation and Retrieval. The goal of FLEURS is to enable speech technology in more languages and catalyze research in low-resource speech understanding.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau, Min Ma, Simran Khanuja, Yu Zhang, Vera Axelrod, Siddharth Dalmia, Jason Riesa, Clara Rivera, Ankur Bapna (Meta AI Research, Google Research, Carnegie Mellon University)
extraction.publisher: Meta AI Research, Google Research, Carnegie Mellon University
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The data collection process starts with the FLoRes-101 dataset, specifically its dev and devtest sets (2009 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and translated into 101 languages by human translators). For each sentence in the 102 languages, three recordings were collected by three different native speakers, with an imposed sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% when possible. Each recording was evaluated by additional workers to assess correspondence to the input sentence, and invalid recordings were discarded. The collected data was split into train, development (dev), and test sets with disjoint speakers, targeting a 7:1:2 ratio. All segments are within 30 seconds. Recordings are kept as-is, from quiet or noisy environments, without data augmentations. The speech sampling rate is 16kHz. FLEURS uses a bottom up approach of collecting spoken utterances for aligned segments, while most other datasets are aligned at a document level with automatic segmentation and alignment for segments. It provides natural human speech and high quality transcripts for each language with strong quality control.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Physical data collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: In the first version of the dataset, about 21.5% of the sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated. We plan to fill these gaps in the future versions of the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: FLoRes-101 dataset (dev and devtest sets), which contains 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and translated into 101 languages by human translators. Speech recordings were collected from native speakers for these sentences.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Transcripts undergo NFC and FST normalization, lower-casing, normalization, and punctuation removal. Words are split into characters, defining tokens as word boundaries. For each sentence, three versions are provided: the original raw transcript (SRC RAW), the preprocessed version (SRC NORM), and its character-based version (SRC CHAR), which should be used for ASR.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Source transcripts are reused from FLoRes-101, which were produced by human translators. Each collected speech recording is evaluated by additional workers to assess whether the recording corresponds to the input sentence.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Three recordings per sentence, each evaluated by additional workers.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Native speakers, with an imposed sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% when possible.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors plan to fill missing data gaps in future versions of the dataset.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender (sex ratio of at least 30/70% was imposed for speakers).
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to catalyze research in few-shot understanding in many languages, enabling progress towards building speech technologies for everyone.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Results are much better on the Western European group than on other groups like Sub-Saharan African or South Asian, partly due to larger amounts of unlabeled data in WE languages from MLS and VoxPopuli. CJK languages are known for the vast number of homophones in speech, adding difficulties in selecting the correct character without language models. For South Asian languages, most substitution errors come from Urdu due to its acoustic similarity to Hindi, leading to transliteration issues. Tokenization mismatch between fine-tuning and pre-training regimes affects CJK languages. Odia (or) is unseen in text pre-training and unrepresented in the tokenizer due to its unique script. Urdu (ur) is unseen in speech pre-training, leading to worse Text-to-Speech retrieval performance due to phonetic closeness to Hindi.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Performance gaps exist across geographical groups, with lower performance on Sub-Saharan African and South Asian languages. Languages unseen by pre-training often show worse performance due to limited supervised data for fine-tuning. CJK languages face difficulties due to homophones and tokenization mismatches. Odia and Urdu show specific limitations related to script representation and phonetic similarity, respectively.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Translation, and Retrieval (Speech-to-Text, Text-to-Speech, cross-lingual, zero-shot capabilities).
